strengths: The paper addresses a practically important NLP question: when it is worth collecting labels and specializing a smaller model instead of relying on zero/few-shot larger LMs for classification. The break-even framing is useful and easy to relate to annotation-budget decisions.

The empirical scope is substantial: 8 datasets with different classification characteristics, multiple model families, fine-tuning, instruction-tuning, prompting, and in-context learning, plus repeated runs to expose variance.
The emphasis on randomness sensitivity is a real strength. Reporting mean and standard deviation across many subsamples/seeds is more informative than the single-run comparisons common in this area.

The paper is generally clear, includes implementation details and hyperparameters in the appendix, acknowledges major limitations, and provides a public code link, which supports reproducibility better than many large-model comparison papers.

The findings about dataset dependence, model-size non-monotonicity, and the limited effect of 4-bit quantization are useful empirical observations for practitioners, even if they are not theoretically deep.
weaknesses: The central headline claim that specialized models need only around 100 labeled examples is not fully supported as stated. Several reported break-even points are far larger, especially for binary datasets and comparisons against in-context learning or instruction-tuned models, and some second break-even points are not reached at all. The paper should qualify this claim more sharply.

The break-even methodology using mean±one standard deviation as a worst/best-case criterion is heuristic and not a principled statistical test. It does not provide confidence intervals over break-even points, paired significance tests, or uncertainty induced by unequal numbers of runs across methods.

The comparison is not fully fair to prompting/ICL: a single prompt, tuned on one model, is used across all models; stronger prompt search, calibration, answer normalization, retrieval-based or validation-selected demonstrations, and modern ICL selection methods are not included. This may change the break-even points substantially.

Some protocol choices risk selection bias or unclear deployment realism. For ICL, the paper reports the best performance achieved up to a dataset subset, which appears oracle-like unless selected on validation data. The best model per approach is also emphasized, which may rely on test-set hindsight.

Data contamination is a serious unresolved threat because the datasets are standard GLUE/SuperGLUE and classic text-classification benchmarks likely present in LLM pretraining. The paper acknowledges this, but the central comparison between general LMs and specialized models remains vulnerable without newer or held-out datasets.

The large-model evaluation is partly cost-limited: GPT is run fewer times, larger models are evaluated on only 1000 test samples, and quantized/non-quantized settings differ by model and approach. These choices weaken claims about variance, model size, and compute efficiency.

The compute-efficiency discussion is approximate and incomplete for practical deployment: FLOPs estimates omit API cost uncertainty, memory/latency, amortization over number of predictions, and the cost of prompt/example selection. This makes some recommendations stronger than the evidence warrants.

The contribution is mainly an empirical synthesis rather than a new method. It is sound and relevant enough for Findings, but the methodological caveats and overgeneralized claims limit confidence for main-conference acceptance.

strengths: The paper asks a practical and NLP-relevant question: when labelled data are scarce, how many labels are needed before specialised smaller models beat general larger LMs on classification tasks?

The empirical scope is fairly broad: multiple datasets, model families, and approaches are compared, including fine-tuning, instruction-tuning, prompting, in-context learning, quantisation, and model-size effects.
The authors correctly emphasize variance and repeated runs, which is often neglected in few-shot comparisons. Reporting break-even points with variance-aware analysis is a useful framing.

The paper provides many implementation details, prompt/verbalizer information, hyperparameters, limitations, and a code link, which supports reproducibility more than many comparable empirical papers.
weaknesses: The central '100 labelled samples on average' claim is over-aggregated and somewhat overstated. The table and plots show very large dataset-dependent variation, many thousands of labels for some binary tasks, and several cases where no variance-aware break-even point is reached.

The variance-aware break-even definition is not statistically rigorous: comparing mean minus one standard deviation to mean plus one standard deviation is not a confidence test, does not justify the stated low-probability interpretation, and is applied across settings with unequal numbers of runs.

The fairness of the comparisons is only partial. A single prompt tuned around Mistral is used for all models; the best model or quantised/full-precision variant is selected for reporting; in-context learning reports the best shot count up to the subset size; and instruction-tuning differs across full tuning and LoRA/quantised setups.

The evidence base is limited to English classification benchmarks, many of which are old and likely represented in pretraining corpora. The paper acknowledges contamination risk, but this substantially weakens claims about general LMs and model-size effects.

The compute-efficiency discussion is under-supported. Approximate FLOP accounting does not fully capture context length, decoding, memory, wall-clock cost, API models, or deployment/inference regimes, yet the recommendations rely on compute-efficiency claims.

The practical recommendations sometimes outrun the evidence, especially the suggestion that instruction-tuning is optimal in broad settings and that quantisation should generally be preferred based on a relatively narrow set of models and tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-scoped NLP question: how many labelled examples are needed before specialised smaller models overtake larger general LMs for text classification. The break-even framing is clear and useful.

The empirical coverage is strong: 8 datasets, several model families and sizes, fine-tuning, instruction-tuning, prompting, and in-context learning, with repeated runs and explicit attention to variance, model size, quantisation, and compute.

The main findings are actionable and appropriately nuanced in places: specialised models can be competitive with modest labels, but the required label count varies sharply by dataset/task, and variance can substantially change the comparison.

Reproducibility is above average because the paper gives prompts, model/training details, dataset split policy, run counts, and an open code repository. The limitations section is also candid about scope, subsampling, prompt choice, and possible contamination.
weaknesses: The headline claim around “100 labelled samples” is somewhat overstated. Several table entries require hundreds to thousands of labels, and some second break-even points are not reached; averaging across heterogeneous datasets and approaches obscures this distribution.

The comparison relies heavily on best-performing model or best-performing shot-count reporting. In-context learning performance is reported as the best achieved up to a dataset subset, which may amount to optimistic selection unless done on validation data. Best-of-approach aggregation also hides model-selection cost.

The variance methodology is useful but informal. Defining the second break-even point via mean plus/minus one standard deviation does not by itself justify claims about low probability; confidence intervals, paired/bootstrap tests, or probability-of-superiority analyses would make this substantially more rigorous.

Prompting fairness is a concern: a single prompt engineered on Mistral-7B is applied across models, while the paper itself notes prompt format is highly influential. This may understate or distort the performance of some general LMs.

Generalisation is limited to English classification benchmarks, many of which are likely present in LLM pretraining. The paper acknowledges possible contamination but does not control for it empirically, which weakens claims about general LMs versus specialised models.

The compute-efficiency analysis is relatively coarse, based mainly on approximate FLOPs. More direct reporting of wall-clock cost, inference amortisation, hardware, token counts, and API costs would better support the practical recommendations.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: how many labeled examples are needed before specialized smaller models become preferable to general-purpose LLM prompting/ICL for text classification.
The empirical scope is strong: 8 datasets, several task types, multiple model families, and comparisons across fine-tuning, instruction-tuning, prompting, and in-context learning.
The repeated-run design and explicit attention to variance are a real contribution. Many empirical LLM comparison papers understate randomness, and the break-even framing is useful for practitioners.

The paper is generally clear, includes prompts, dataset details, hyperparameters, compute estimates, limitations, and a public code link, supporting reproducibility better than many comparable empirical studies.

The main findings are nuanced rather than purely promotional: the authors identify strong dependence on dataset/task characteristics, cases where LLMs remain competitive, and limits caused by possible pretraining contamination.
weaknesses: The central “100 labeled samples on average” claim risks being overemphasized: the paper itself shows very wide variation, including binary datasets where thousands of examples may be required or where variance-aware break-even is not reached.

The variance-aware break-even criterion based on mean +/- one standard deviation is a heuristic, not a statistical confidence interval or paired significance test. This weakens the rigor of claims about robust superiority, especially with only 20 runs for most non-fine-tuning approaches and 10 for GPT.

The comparison is sensitive to prompt and ICL design, but the study uses a single manually engineered prompt template rather than model-specific optimized prompts or prompt ensembles. This may understate general LLM performance and affects the fairness claim.

Possible benchmark contamination is a substantial unresolved issue for common datasets such as SST-2, AG News, TREC, SNIPS, and DBpedia. The authors acknowledge this, but it still limits causal interpretation of general-vs-specialized comparisons.

The compute-efficiency discussion is useful but approximate. FLOPs estimates do not fully capture wall-clock cost, batching, API cost, inference amortization, LoRA settings, quantization implementation details, or practical deployment constraints.

Some experimental choices need sharper justification: using random 60/20/20 splits rather than standard benchmark splits, evaluating large models on sampled test sets, and reporting the best ICL performance over available shot counts could all affect the estimated break-even points.

The contribution is primarily an empirical synthesis and recommendation paper rather than a new method. Given related prior work on fine-tuning vs ICL and data efficiency, the novelty is moderate despite the breadth and variance analysis.

The break-even criterion based on mean plus/minus one standard deviation is not a statistically principled test of superiority. It conflates run variance with uncertainty, does not use paired comparisons or confidence intervals, and makes the “worst-case” interpretation stronger than the evidence warrants.

The break-even framing is useful and more actionable than reporting isolated few-shot/full-data results.

The paper is generally transparent about experimental details, including prompts, label verbalisers, splits, hyperparameters, numbers of runs, compute estimates, and limitations. Releasing code further supports reproducibility.

The main qualitative conclusions are mostly supported: specialized models are often competitive with surprisingly few labeled examples; variance can materially change comparisons; dataset/task properties matter; and larger models are not uniformly better in this classification setting.

The discussion gives practical recommendations that follow naturally from the experiments and acknowledges important constraints such as task contamination, prompt dependence, evaluation cost, and restriction to English classification tasks.
weaknesses: The central headline claim that specialized models need about 100 labeled examples is too coarse relative to the reported heterogeneity. The variance-aware break-even criterion uses mean minus/plus one standard deviation as a proxy for worst/best cases and low probability, but this is not a formal confidence interval or statistical test. Since run counts differ across approaches, especially 100 fine-tuning runs vs. 20 LLM runs vs. 10 GPT runs, comparisons of uncertainty are only partially controlled.

The in-context learning protocol appears to report the best performance over possible numbers of examples up to the available subset. If this selection is made using test performance, it introduces an oracle advantage; if selected otherwise, the selection procedure needs to be made explicit. This affects the validity of break-even points.

The comparison is sensitive to prompt design, but the main experiments use a single prompt optimized around one model family. This is acknowledged, but it remains a major threat to conclusions about general LLM performance, especially across Flan-T5, LLaMA, Mistral/Zephyr, and GPT-style models.

Some recommendations therefore rest on weaker evidence than the performance claims.

The paper is an empirical comparison rather than a methodological advance. It is sound and useful enough for Findings, but the limitations above and the dependence on many design choices make the case for main-conference acceptance borderline at best.

strengths: Clear, practically important question for NLP: when it is worth labeling data and specializing smaller models instead of relying on larger general LMs for text classification.
Broad empirical comparison across fine-tuning, instruction-tuning, prompting, and in-context learning, with multiple model families, dataset types, and model sizes.
The repeated-run design and variance-aware break-even analysis are valuable; the paper correctly shows that few-shot conclusions can change substantially once randomness is considered.
Appendices give useful experimental detail, the paper discusses compute and quantization, and the code release materially improves reproducibility.
The discussion is grounded and actionable, especially in distinguishing cases where general LMs remain useful from cases where small specialized models are preferable.
weaknesses: The headline claim around "100 labelled samples" is too compressed and risks overstatement: many break-even points are in the hundreds, thousands, or unavailable, especially for binary tasks and comparisons against ICL or instruction-tuned models.

The mean-plus/minus-standard-deviation break-even criterion is a useful heuristic but not a formal statistical guarantee; confidence intervals, paired tests, or bootstrap analyses would make the variance claims stronger.

The prompting/ICL comparison may be sensitive to design choices: a single prompt tuned on one model is reused across models, and the procedure for choosing the best number of in-context examples is not fully separated from evaluation.
Benchmark contamination, random 60/20/20 splits instead of official splits, and 1000-example evaluation subsampling could materially affect the reported break-even points.
Compute-efficiency claims rely on approximate FLOP accounting and are confounded by architecture, LoRA vs full tuning, quantization choices, API model behavior, and deployment assumptions.

The scope is limited to English classification benchmarks, so the recommendations should not be read as applying broadly to generation, multilingual tasks, long-context settings, or newer proprietary LMs.
